notes.1a: Almost all candidates were able to obtain the expected results showing an increase in temperature followed by a decrease.
notes.1b: A number of errors in plotting were noted. Most candidates followed the instruction to draw two intersecting straight lines. Some candidates did ‘dot to dot’ lines or curves. Some candidates are plotted points or drew graph lines in ink – this means that if an error is made the point/line that is wrong cannot be erased.
notes.1c: Almost all candidates were able to obtain the expected results showing an increase in temperature followed by a decrease.
notes.1d: A number of errors in plotting were found and some candidates ignored the instruction to draw two intersecting straight lines.
notes.1e: (i) A number of candidates misread their graph scales despite having just successfully plotted the graph. A small number of answers stated the temperature rather than the volume.
notes.1eii: Most candidates worked out that a smaller volume would be required; they did not go on to give a quantitative answer and reason.
notes.1f: Candidates need to ensure that when writing exothermic that the ‘x’ does not look like an ‘n’ as the intended answer must be unambiguous.
notes.1g: (i) Almost all candidates realised that the burette needed to be cleaned, with most candidates focussing on the acid left from the previous experiment.
notes.1gii: Many candidates focused on removing the acid from the previous experiment despite having already removed it with water. Only the better performing candidates realised the water would dilute the acid used in the second experiment and so had to be removed.
notes.1h: Many candidates did not realise that a source of error is not removed by repeating an experiment – if the same method and apparatus is used then that source of error in still there. Better responses identified heat loss or using a measuring cylinder as a source of error.
notes.2a: (i) A number of candidates confused flame test with testing a gas with a lighted splint. The result of a flame test should be a colour, not ‘the flame went out’.
notes.2aii: Most candidates gave an acceptable pH value.
notes.2b: By this stage candidates could have identified solution T as aqueous sodium hydroxide. The results given by some candidates suggested that having worked out this was the reaction between an aqueous zinc salt and aqueous sodium hydroxide all that they needed to do was give observations similar to those in the Notes for use in qualitative analysis. However, in this instance the tests were reversed, with the zinc salt being added to the sodium hydroxide. Almost all candidates missed the initial formation of a white precipitate, which then quickly dissolves before any more of the zinc salt is added.
notes.2c: The gas given off should have been ammonia. Some candidates reported positive tests for chlorine, presumably thinking that because ammonium chloride was used that chlorine would be made, it is not possible for chlorine to be made in this way. The expected test and result was that for ammonia.
notes.2d: Many candidates missed the initial green precipitate, which rapidly dissolves giving a green solution. The final green precipitate that should have been formed when excess was added was often reported as being a green solution.
notes.2e: Most candidates could correctly identify solution T.
notes.2f: Most candidates stated that liquid U was colourless. It should be noted that ‘clear’ is not accepted as an alternative to colourless; coloured solutions, such as aqueous copper(II) sulfate, are coloured and clear.
notes.2g: Many candidates noted the formation of a yellow precipitate.
notes.2h: Most candidates reported that liquid U caught fire, some incorrectly stated that it extinguished the lighted splint.
notes.2i: A common error was to state that liquid U contained iodide ions; this was presumably because of the yellow precipitate seen in Question 2(g), despite the fact that silver nitrate had not been used.
notes.3: This question required candidates to extract the mixture of pigments from the leaves and then to analyse the pigments. Unfortunately, most answers seen concentrated on either extracting the pigment from the leaves or on conducting chromatography rather than addressing both aspects; relatively few answers described how to obtain the pigment from the leaves and then conduct chromatography. It was not uncommon for candidates who missed out the pigment extraction stage to place the leaf directly on chromatography paper. Some candidates were not sure what to do with the sand and so used it as a filtration medium or even the stationary phase in chromatography.
